paragraphs: Enter Sampson and Gregory, armed with swords and small shields.
SAMPSON. Gregory, I swear, we won’t put up with insults.
GREGORY. No, because then we’d be pushed around like coal carriers.
SAMPSON. I mean, if we get angry, we’ll draw our swords.
GREGORY. Sure, while you’re alive, pull your neck out of the noose.
SAMPSON. I hit fast once I’m provoked.
GREGORY. But you’re not quick to be provoked into hitting.
SAMPSON. A dog from the house of Montague provokes me.
GREGORY. To be provoked is to move, and to be brave is to stand your ground. So if you’re provoked, you run away.
SAMPSON. A dog from that house will make me stand my ground. I’ll take the wall from any man or maid of the Montagues.
GREGORY. That shows you’re a weakling, because the weakest get pushed to the wall.
SAMPSON. True, and that’s why women, being the weaker vessels, are always shoved against the wall. So I’ll shove the Montague men away from the wall and push their maids up against it.
GREGORY. The quarrel is between our masters and us, their men.
SAMPSON. It’s all the same. I’ll show myself a tyrant. When I’ve fought the men, I’ll be nice to the maids: I’ll cut off their heads.
GREGORY. The heads of the maids?
SAMPSON. Yes, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads. Take it whichever way you like.
GREGORY. They’ll have to take it in whatever way they feel it.
SAMPSON. They’ll feel me as long as I can stand. And everyone knows I’m a fine piece of flesh.
GREGORY. It’s a good thing you’re not a fish. If you were, you’d be a poor, dried-up one. Draw your weapon. Here come some of the house of Montague.
Enter Abram and Balthasar.
SAMPSON. My sword is out. Start a quarrel, and I’ll back you up.
GREGORY. How? Turn your back and run?
SAMPSON. Don’t worry about me.
GREGORY. No, indeed. I’m worried about you!
SAMPSON. Let’s keep the law on our side. Let them start it.
GREGORY. I’ll frown as I pass by, and they can take it however they like.
SAMPSON. No, however they dare. I’ll bite my thumb at them, which is an insult if they put up with it.
ABRAM. Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON. I am biting my thumb, sir.
ABRAM. Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON. (aside to Gregory) Is the law on our side if I say yes?
GREGORY. No.
SAMPSON. No, sir, I’m not biting my thumb at you, sir. But I am biting my thumb, sir.
GREGORY. Are you looking for a fight, sir?
ABRAM. A fight, sir? No, sir.
SAMPSON. But if you are, sir, I’m ready for you. I serve a man as good as yours.
ABRAM. No better.
SAMPSON. Well, sir.
Enter Benvolio.
GREGORY. (aside to Sampson) Say “better.” Here comes one of my master’s relatives.
SAMPSON. Yes, better, sir.
ABRAM. You lie.
SAMPSON. Draw, if you’re men. Gregory, remember your big swing.
[They fight.]
BENVOLIO. Break it up, fools! Put away your swords. You don’t know what you’re doing.
[He beats down their swords.]
Enter Tybalt.
TYBALT. What, you’ve drawn your sword among these cowardly servants? Turn around, Benvolio, and look at your death.
BENVOLIO. I’m only keeping the peace. Put away your sword, or use it to help me separate these men.
TYBALT. What, sword drawn and you talk of peace? I hate that word as I hate hell, all Montagues, and you. Have at you, coward!
[They fight.]
Enter three or four Citizens with clubs.
FIRST CITIZEN. Clubs, spears, and pikes! Strike! Beat them down! Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
Enter Capulet in his dressing gown, and Lady Capulet.
CAPULET. What’s all this noise? Give me my long sword, quick!
LADY CAPULET. A crutch, a crutch! Why do you call for a sword?
CAPULET. My sword, I say! Old Montague has come, and he’s waving his blade to spite me.
Enter Montague and his wife, Lady Montague.
MONTAGUE. You villain Capulet! Don’t hold me back, let me go.
LADY MONTAGUE. You will not take one step to look for an enemy.
Enter Prince Escalus, with attendants.

PRINCE. Rebellious subjects, enemies of peace, you who dishonor this blade stained with your neighbors’ blood. Won’t they listen? Hey! You men, you beasts, who quench the fire of your destructive rage with purple fountains spurting from your veins, on pain of torture, throw your misused weapons to the ground from your bloody hands and hear the sentence of your angry prince. Three civil brawls, bred from a casual word, between you, old Capulet, and Montague, have three times disturbed the quiet of our streets and forced Verona’s elderly citizens to lay aside their dignified dress to wield old spears in hands as old, rusted with peace, to part your rusted hatred. If you ever disturb our streets again, your lives will pay the price for the peace. For now, all the rest of you leave. You, Capulet, will come with me, and Montague, you come this afternoon to learn our further decision on this matter at Old Free-town, our common court of justice. Once more, on pain of death, everyone leave.
[Exit Prince and attendants; Capulet, Lady Capulet, Tybalt, Citizens, and servants.]
MONTAGUE. Who started this old quarrel up again? Speak, nephew. Were you there when it began?

BENVOLIO. Your enemy’s servants and yours were already fighting hand to hand before I arrived. I drew my sword to separate them, and at that moment fiery Tybalt came with his sword ready. As he breathed defiance in my ears, he swung it around his head and cut the wind, which, unharmed, hissed at him in scorn. While we were trading thrusts and blows, more and more people came and fought on one side and the other, until the Prince came and parted them.
LADY MONTAGUE. Oh, where is Romeo? Did you see him today? I’m very glad he wasn’t in this fight.

BENVOLIO. Madam, an hour before the worshipped sun peeped out of the golden window of the east, a troubled mind drove me out to walk. Under the grove of sycamores that grows on the west side of the city, I saw your son walking that early. I headed toward him, but he noticed me and slipped into the cover of the woods. I, judging his feelings by my own, which most wanted to be where no one could be found, being one too many even for my weary self, followed my own mood without chasing his, and gladly avoided him, who was gladly avoiding me.

MONTAGUE. Many a morning he’s been seen there, adding tears to the fresh morning dew and more clouds to the clouds with his deep sighs. But as soon as the all-cheering sun starts to draw the shady curtains from Aurora’s bed in the far east, my heavy-hearted son steals home away from the light, shuts himself up alone in his room, closes his windows, locks out the fair daylight, and makes himself an artificial night. This mood will prove black and ominous unless good advice can remove its cause.
BENVOLIO. My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
MONTAGUE. I don’t know it, and I can’t learn it from him.
BENVOLIO. Have you pressed him in any way?

MONTAGUE. Both myself and many other friends. But he, the counselor of his own feelings, is so secret and closed up, so far from being sounded out or discovered, like a bud bitten by a jealous worm before it can spread its sweet leaves to the air or dedicate its beauty to the sun. If we could only learn where his sorrows come from, we would be as willing to cure them as to know them.
Enter Romeo.
BENVOLIO. Look, here he comes. If you please, step aside. I’ll find out his trouble, or be very much refused.
MONTAGUE. I hope you’re lucky enough by staying to hear his true confession. Come, madam, let’s go.
[Exit Montague and Lady Montague.]
BENVOLIO. Good morning, cousin.
ROMEO. Is the day so young?
BENVOLIO. It just struck nine.
ROMEO. Oh, sad hours seem long. Was that my father who left so quickly?
BENVOLIO. It was. What sadness makes Romeo’s hours so long?
ROMEO. Not having what, if I had it, would make them short.
BENVOLIO. In love?
ROMEO. Out.
BENVOLIO. Of love?
ROMEO. Out of her favor, where I’m in love.
BENVOLIO. What a shame that love, so gentle to look at, should be so tyrannical and rough when tested.

ROMEO. What a shame that love, whose eyes are always blindfolded, can find paths to what it wants without eyes! Where shall we eat? Oh, me! What fight was here? Don’t tell me, because I’ve heard it all. There’s a lot going on here about hate, but more about love. So, oh, brawling love! Oh, loving hate! Oh, anything created first out of nothing! Oh, heavy lightness! Serious vanity! Misshapen chaos of good-looking forms! Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health! Always-waking sleep, which is not what it is! This is the love I feel, who feel no love in this. Don’t you laugh?
BENVOLIO. No, cousin, I’d rather weep.
ROMEO. Good heart, at what?
BENVOLIO. At the burden on your good heart.

ROMEO. Why, that’s what love does. My own griefs lie heavy on my chest, and you’ll add to them by pressing them down with more of yours. This love you’ve shown adds more grief to my already too much. Love is a smoke made from the fumes of sighs. When cleared, it’s a fire sparkling in lovers’ eyes. When troubled, it’s a sea fed by lovers’ tears. What else is it? A most careful madness, a choking bitterness, and a preserving sweetness. Goodbye, my cousin.
[Going.]
BENVOLIO. Wait! I’ll go along with you. If you leave me like this, you do me wrong.
ROMEO. Bah! I’ve lost myself. I’m not here. This isn’t Romeo. He’s somewhere else.
BENVOLIO. Tell me seriously, who is it you love?
ROMEO. What, should I groan and tell you?
BENVOLIO. Groan! Why, no. But seriously tell me who.
ROMEO. Telling a sick man seriously to make his will is a poor request for someone so ill. Seriously, cousin, I love a woman.
BENVOLIO. I aimed that close when I guessed you were in love.
ROMEO. A very good marksman. And the one I love is beautiful.
BENVOLIO. A beautiful target, dear cousin, is the easiest to hit.

ROMEO. Well, you miss in that hit. She won’t be hit by Cupid’s arrow. She has the wit of Diana. Well armed in strong proof of chastity, she lives unaffected by love’s weak, childish bow. She won’t endure the siege of loving words, nor stand the encounter of assailing eyes, nor open her lap to saint-seducing gold. Oh, she’s rich in beauty, only poor in that when she dies, her riches die with her beauty.
BENVOLIO. Then she’s sworn to stay chaste forever?

ROMEO. She has, and in that saving, she wastes enormously. For beauty starved by her severity cuts off beauty from all future generations. She’s too beautiful, too wise, wisely too beautiful, to earn her heaven by making me despair. She’s sworn off love, and in that vow I live as if dead, I who live to tell it now.
BENVOLIO. Take my advice: forget about her.
ROMEO. Oh, teach me how to forget how to think.
BENVOLIO. By giving your eyes freedom. Look at other beauties.

ROMEO. That’s the way to make hers, so exquisite, stand out even more. These fortunate masks that kiss fair ladies’ brows, being black, remind us that they hide the beauty beneath. A man who’s struck blind can’t forget the precious treasure of the sight he’s lost. Show me a mistress who’s exceptionally beautiful. What does her beauty serve but as a note where I can read who surpassed that exceptional beauty? Goodbye. You can’t teach me to forget.
BENVOLIO. I’ll prove that lesson right, or die in debt.
[Exit.]
